narration: It was a night when the stars shone beautifully. I remember a boy once standing atop a hill on a night like this. It is a memory so distant it feels more like a half-forgotten dream.

I used to hate the night. Nightfall brought a specific kind of silence—one that felt heavy and sharp with cold. I’d slip between the frozen sheets, feeling the vast, ink-black space of the room pressing in on me. Even with my eyelids squeezed shut, the darkness felt alive, keeping rest just out of reach.  I would brace myself against the dark and pray for the morning to come.

One night, a strange light flickered against my eyelids. It felt different from the usual pale shimmer of the moon. Driven by curiosity, I opened my eyes. Outside my window, a single beam of light descended from the heavens like a silken thread, landing on a remote hill at the edge of town.
I watched until the glow began to fade. By the time I rubbed my sleepy eyes, it was gone. Still half-dreaming, I slipped out of the house and made my way toward the outskirts of town.

As I climbed the hill, I saw him—a boy who looked to be about my age. Despite the summer season, the air at this altitude turned biting once the sun went down. Yet, he wore nothing but a single layer of tattered, thin clothes. He didn't seem to feel the cold at all.

"Hello there," he said.
He raised a hand in greeting the moment he saw me cresting the ridge. His simple, honest smile instantly dissolved my wariness. I ended up staying there with him until the sun rose. After that night, I found myself returning to the hill again and again just to see him.

"Good evening. You came back," he would say, greeting me formally every time I reached the summit. I would offer a small, shy reply.
"The stars are beautiful again tonight," he’d remark.
He only ever appeared on nights when the stars were bright.

We would lie together in the grass, gazing up at the sky. We watched the stars glitter in the cold, crystalline air while the ground beneath us grew as chilled as ice. Eventually, I began bringing thicker clothes and a light blanket. Bundled up together, the blanket felt warmer than usual. My fear of the dark and my lingering anxieties seemed to melt away under the vastness of the stars.

As we watched the sky, he would tell me stories.
"There is another world on the far side of the starlight." It was a story he told often, and one I never grew tired of hearing. "In that world, day and night are reversed. When it is night here, it is high noon there. When the sun shines on us, they are draped in darkness."

I would hum in agreement, listening intently. I was mostly the listener in our pair; he seemed to love the act of spinning tales, and I loved asking questions about the things that piqued my interest. It was a comfortable rhythm for us both.

"And in that world," he continued, "the sky is held up by a person. Just one person, standing with their hands toward the sky. They have to, you see. If they didn’t, the sky and all its stars would come crashing down. Someone has to carry the weight."

I must have looked skeptical because he began to explain further, as if gently untying a knot.
"I suppose it's hard for you to imagine the sky falling. You’ve never seen it happen in this world, have you? That is a rare and beautiful blessing."
I still didn't quite understand.

"You see," he said, "the sky is supported by the people who look up at it. In your world, there are so many people looking up, sending their thoughts into the ether—just like we are now. People entrust their deepest wishes to that fading light. Anyone who looks at the stars feels a stir of emotion, a prayer that tomorrow will come safely. The sheer strength of all those individual hearts is enough to keep the stars from falling."

"Then... does no one look at the stars in the other world?" I asked, tilting my head.
"In that world," he replied softly, "the stars are believed to be reflections of the dead. They are things to be watched over by, not things to be looked at. They say that only those close to death—those who sense their time is coming—look at the stars. So, the healthy and the vibrant turn away from the night. They huddle in their beds and try to forget the darkness exists."

In my world, we all shared the burden. In his, one person stood alone.
"Isn't it lonely?" I whispered.
"Of course it is. To stand alone all night, every night. And you have to be as close to the sky as possible, so you must stand on the highest mountain peak. The air is freezing, the wind is a gale, and the sky itself... it is incredibly heavy. An ordinary person wouldn't last a single day."

"Then why doesn't that person just run away?"
A shadow of a pained expression crossed his face. "Because it is his punishment. A weight they must carry to atone for their sins."
"Did he do something that terrible?"
"Sometimes," he said, "even protecting your family can be seen as a crime. Values and perspectives change as the eras pass. In the flow of time, he was blamed, branded a sinner, and cast out."
